claims.normalized_claim: In Carroll v. United States (1925) the Supreme Court held that officers may search an automobile without a warrant if they have probable cause to believe it contains contraband subject to seizure, because a vehicle can be quickly moved out of the jurisdiction in which a warrant would have to be sought — creating what is known as the 'automobile exception' to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement.
evidence_locations: Carroll, Opinion of the Court (Taft, C.J.), holding + mobility rationale
counterevidence: McReynolds, J., joined by Sutherland, J., dissented.
allowed_wording: Since 1925, police have been allowed to search your car without a warrant — if they have probable cause it contains contraband — because a car can be driven away before a warrant could be obtained.
prohibited_wording: Police can search your car any time.
Police never need a warrant for anything in a car.
claims.notes: The core 'automobile exception'. Requires probable cause (see CLM-0003).

claims.normalized_claim: Carroll arose during Prohibition: George Carroll and John Kiro were convicted of transporting bonded whisky and gin, and federal agents who stopped their car on the highway found 68 bottles of liquor hidden behind the upholstery of the seats.
counterevidence: Some summaries paraphrase the count/location loosely; the opinion supports 68 bottles behind the upholstery.
allowed_wording: It started with bootleggers: agents tore into the seats of a car and pulled out 68 bottles of illegal liquor.
prohibited_wording: State a precise vote count as opinion-verbatim (report Carroll as decided 6-2 only as commonly reported).
claims.notes: Vote reported 6-2 (Taft majority; McReynolds+Sutherland dissent; Stone did not participate) — treat numeric tally as 'reported'.

claims.normalized_claim: The automobile exception requires probable cause — a fair probability that the vehicle contains contraband or evidence — not merely a hunch or reasonable suspicion; a routine traffic stop by itself does not authorize a full search of the car.
evidence_locations: Labron ('probable cause exists to believe it contains contraband')
allowed_wording: The power isn't unlimited: police need probable cause, a real reason to believe there's contraband — being pulled over, by itself, is not a search warrant for your whole car.
prohibited_wording: A hunch is enough for police to search your car.
Any traffic stop lets police search your entire car.
claims.notes: Key myth-correction; drives the second-person 'here's the real line' payoff.

claims.normalized_claim: When the automobile exception applies, its scope is defined by the object of the search: police may look anywhere in the vehicle — including closed containers, bags, and the trunk — where there is probable cause to believe that object could be found (United States v. Ross, 1982; California v. Acevedo, 1991).
allowed_wording: If they have probable cause, the search can reach wherever that item could be — the glovebox, the trunk, a bag on the back seat, a closed container.
prohibited_wording: They can search anything anywhere with no limit.
claims.notes: Scope bounded by probable cause + object, not unlimited.

claims.normalized_claim: The automobile exception has no separate exigency requirement beyond the car's ready mobility: if a vehicle is readily mobile and there is probable cause it contains contraband, police may search it without a warrant, without proving any additional emergency (Pennsylvania v. Labron, 1996; Maryland v. Dyson, 1999).
evidence_locations: Labron (readily mobile + probable cause = search 'without more')
allowed_wording: The Court has said police don't even have to prove a separate emergency — a car being drivable, plus probable cause, is enough.
claims.notes: Explains why the exception is so broad in practice.

claims.normalized_claim: In Collins v. Virginia, an officer investigating an orange-and-black motorcycle that had eluded police walked up the driveway of the home where Ryan Collins was staying, lifted a tarp covering the motorcycle parked next to the house, ran its plate and identification number, confirmed it was stolen, and then arrested Collins.
allowed_wording: An officer walked up a driveway, lifted a tarp off a motorcycle parked beside the house, and confirmed it was stolen.
prohibited_wording: Depict Ryan Collins' or the officer's real likeness; describe them beyond the record; imply guilt beyond the charge.

claims.normalized_claim: In Collins v. Virginia (decided May 29, 2018, by an 8-1 vote, Justice Sotomayor writing for the majority and Justice Alito dissenting alone), the Supreme Court held that the automobile exception does not permit an officer to enter the curtilage of a home — the area immediately surrounding the house, such as this driveway — to search a vehicle parked there without a warrant; curtilage receives full Fourth Amendment protection. The Court wrote that 'the scope of the automobile exception extends no further than the automobile itself.'
evidence_locations: Collins, Opinion of the Court (Sotomayor, J.), holding + quoted line
counterevidence: Alito, J., dissented; Thomas, J., concurred while questioning the exclusionary remedy.
allowed_wording: The one place they still can't go: your home's curtilage. In 2018 the Court, 8-1, said the car-search power stops at the car — it can't be used to walk onto the ground next to your house.
'The scope of the automobile exception extends no further than the automobile itself.'
prohibited_wording: Say police can never search a car in a driveway (they may with a warrant or another exception).
claims.notes: The payoff / bright line. Vote 8-1 confirmed (was mis-summarized 7-1 by one secondary source).

claims.normalized_claim: Separately from the automobile exception, Arizona v. Gant (2009, 5-4, Justice Stevens) limits searching a car incident to a recent occupant's arrest: police may search the passenger compartment only if the arrestee is unsecured and within reaching distance of it, or it is reasonable to believe the vehicle contains evidence of the offense of arrest.
counterevidence: Four Justices dissented, favoring a broader search-incident rule.
allowed_wording: And arresting you isn't a blank check either: after Gant, once you're handcuffed and away from the car, they generally can't search it just because they arrested you.
prohibited_wording: Conflate Gant (search incident to arrest) with the automobile exception.
claims.notes: Distinct doctrine; include as a limit, keep separate from auto exception.

claims.normalized_claim: In Byrd v. United States (2018, unanimous, Justice Kennedy) the Court held that a driver in lawful possession or control of a rental car generally has a reasonable expectation of privacy in it, even if he or she is not listed as an authorized driver on the rental agreement.
allowed_wording: Even in a rental you're not officially listed on, the Court said in 2018 you can still have privacy the Fourth Amendment protects.

claims.normalized_claim: Whether the smell of marijuana alone gives police probable cause to search a car is not settled by a single nationwide Supreme Court rule; it is jurisdiction-specific and evolving, and several state high courts in places that have legalized or decriminalized cannabis have held that odor alone no longer automatically establishes probable cause.
evidence_locations: No controlling U.S. Supreme Court holding sets a blanket rule (flagged by research).
counterevidence: Historically, in many jurisdictions odor was treated as sufficient; the law is in flux.
allowed_wording: One thing the Supreme Court hasn't settled with a single national rule: whether the smell of marijuana alone is enough — and in states that legalized it, some courts now say it isn't. It depends on where you are.
prohibited_wording: State a blanket national rule that marijuana odor always (or never) justifies a search.
Assert this as settled Supreme Court law.
claims.notes: Grade B / no primary SCOTUS source by design — present ONLY as unsettled/state-dependent, never as a rule. Advertiser-safe, neutral.

findings: 10 claims CLM-0001..0010 graded/source-linked. Collins locked 8-1 (Sotomayor majority, Alito sole dissent). CLM-0010 marijuana-odor grade B, status conditional = present only as unsettled/state-dependent.
